sources.title: A. D. H. Bivar, The Indus Lands, Cambridge Ancient History
sources.note: Cambridge synthesis placing Vatsa upstream on the Yamuna, identifying Kaushambi as its capital and describing Magadha's eventual supremacy.

sources.title: University of Delhi, History of India from Earliest Times up to c. 300 CE
sources.note: University teaching volume on Vatsa, Kaushambi, Udayana traditions, inter-state conflicts, urbanization and the limits of literary evidence.

sources.title: INFLIBNET, Mahajanapadas and the Rise of Magadha
sources.note: University module on Vatsa among the mahajanapadas, Udayana traditions, Kaushambi, monarchy and northern state competition.

sources.title: NIOS, From Janapadas to Empire
sources.note: National Institute of Open Schooling survey of territorial states, agriculture, iron, trade, cities, taxation and armies.

sources.title: G. R. Sharma, Excavations at Kausambi 1949-50, Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India 74
sources.note: Official excavation report on houses, roads, drainage devices, terracotta objects, gamesmen, grooming containers and long site chronology.

sources.title: G. R. Sharma, The Excavations at Kausambi 1957-59: The Defences and the Syenaciti of the Purusamedha
sources.note: University of Allahabad excavation report documenting the defensive sequence, habitation depth, gates, ramparts and material evidence.

sources.title: P. A. Eltsov, The Ancient Indian City and the Thought Expressed in It
sources.note: Peer-reviewed reassessment dating Kaushambi urban authority, defenses, weapons, coins and major structural activity mainly to the sixth through fourth centuries BCE.

sources.title: Satuluri and others, Ground penetrating radar investigations at ancient Panchala and Vatsa capitals
sources.note: Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports study using non-destructive survey to identify buried structural anomalies at Kaushambi while emphasizing the need for archaeological interpretation.

sources.title: INFLIBNET, Iron and Urbanization
sources.note: University archaeology module on early historic farming, settlement growth, iron technologies, pottery, crafts and exchange.

sources.title: INFLIBNET, Iron Age Society and Economy
sources.note: University archaeology module on tools, craft specialization, ceramic manufacture, mixed subsistence and social interpretation.

sources.title: NIOS, The Vedic Age
sources.note: National Institute of Open Schooling survey used cautiously for family, hierarchy, women, food, farming and education background.

sources.title: NIOS, Ancient India Culture and Heritage
sources.note: National Institute of Open Schooling synthesis of homes, foods, clothing, ornaments, occupations, animals, crafts and play.

sources.title: NIOS, Education, Science and Technology, Medicine
sources.note: National Institute of Open Schooling overview of oral learning, teacher-pupil education and the long development of medicine.

sources.title: UNESCO, Tradition of Vedic chanting
sources.note: Authoritative account of childhood training, tonal accents, recitation techniques and long oral preservation.

sources.title: B. V. Subbarayappa, Physicians of ancient India
sources.note: Peer-reviewed medical history distinguishing early healing practices and Buddhist evidence from later compiled Ayurvedic texts.

sources.title: SuttaCentral, Kosambiya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 48, Pali root text
sources.note: Digital canonical Pali text whose opening locates the discourse at Kosambi in Ghosita's monastery.

sources.title: SuttaCentral, Kosambiya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 48, English translation
sources.note: Modern scholarly translation of a Kosambi monastic quarrel and teaching about concord.

sources.title: SuttaCentral, Udena Sutta, Udana 7.10
sources.note: Canonical literary tradition set at Kosambi concerning King Udena, Queen Samavati and women of the palace.

sources.title: SuttaCentral, Kosambakakkhandhaka, Khandhaka 10
sources.note: Vinaya tradition about the Kosambi monastic dispute, daily discipline, water vessels, lavatory conduct and reconciliation.

sources.title: National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities, Central Antiquity Collection objects from Kausambi
sources.note: Official collection listing of Kausambi terracottas including animal figures, a female bust and a toy-chariot fragment, generally without secure displayed dates.

sources.title: National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities, Kausambi stone and bead objects
sources.note: Official collection listing of beads, pendants, stone objects and animal figures from Kausambi, with limited online context.

sources.title: E. Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka, Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum I
sources.note: Government of India epigraphic edition with plate, damaged text, transcription and translation of the Kaushambi edict.

sources.title: Unicode Consortium, Brahmi code chart
sources.note: Official character chart used to label the readable Brahmi line as a modern Unicode normalization rather than a facsimile.

sources.title: Treccani, Kaushambi
sources.note: Scholarly reference entry distinguishing excavated phases, revised chronology, Udayana memory and later history of the city.

proposedOverrides.summary: A compact Yamuna janapada centered on Kaushambi, whose one-century atlas shape and Magadha seam are more exact than its surviving political chronology.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact imported id vatsa is indexed circa 500 to 400 BCE and was missing both a card and researched override at the initial audit.
The card treats Vatsa as a late mahajanapada snapshot centered on Kaushambi and keeps the city's longer archaeological life separate.
No appliesTo alias is added. The broad vedic-aryans layer and separately indexed Kuru, Pancala, Kasi, Kosala, Surasena, Avanti, Magadha and Maurya records remain distinct.
The sole Vatsa geometry is one 16-position Polygon with SHA-256 18d50a39cc51acca2c5de45fa08eee33f04a051810c0ff12c76423fedbcda456.
The imported shape includes tested Kaushambi, Pabhosa, Kara and Fatehpur but excludes Prayagraj and Jhusi, a material map-history mismatch.
The periods cover only the exact 500 to 400 BCE display window and are explicitly reading lenses rather than invented ruler accessions.

The structured ending is uncertain at the 400 BCE seam. Magadha owns every formerly inside test point, but no successor link is asserted because historical accounts differ over the route and timing of absorption.
The written-language sample is a third-century BCE Ashokan Prakrit line addressed to officers at Kosambi, shown in normalized Brahmi Unicode with damage, date and successor-context caveats.
